\subsection{Confirmatory: the limit tracks periodicity, not length}

Figure~\ref{fig:main}(a) is the paper's sharpest test. Each control carries its
twin's carrier and word count, the $k$ copies of one word becoming non-adjacent
distinct ones. Were the failure about length, attention span, exposure bias or a
duration budget, the two curves would coincide. They do not. Below $k\!=\!6$
every model is essentially exact; above it, repeated items are rendered with a
median count error of \ErrRepCk{}\% per checkpoint against \ErrCtl{}\%
$[\ErrCtlLo{},\ErrCtlHi{}]$ for controls ($n=\ErrCtlN{}$), at every $k$ to $32$
and for every model. The contrast is sharpest in exactly-correct renderings:
\ExactCtl{}\% for controls against \ExactRep{}\% for their twins. Decoders that
miscount a repeated sequence five times in six render its non-adjacent twin
right nineteen times in twenty. Controls are not perfect --- \CtlMissPct{}\%
carry genuine truncations --- but they are exact where their twins are not.

\emph{Our \NModels{} checkpoints are only \NFamilies{} architecture families},
so we model the clustering rather than count checkpoints. By family the gap is
\FamExact{} points $[\FamExactLo{},\FamExactHi{}]$, all three positive; by
checkpoint \CkExact{} $[\CkExactLo{},\CkExactHi{}]$, positive in all
\CkExactNPos{} --- including the checkpoint whose median-error gap is zero,
which still renders repeated items exactly \CkRevExact{} points less often than
its controls (Table~\ref{tab:models}). A mixed-effects linear probability model
with architecture as a random effect, checkpoint nested inside it, stimulus
crossed and a family-varying arm slope puts the gap at \MixArm{} points;
\MixAllClear{} six interval constructions exclude zero, the widest ---
cluster-robust at the checkpoint level --- being $[\MixLo{},\MixHi{}]$. Partial
pooling answers the question three families cannot answer directly: the
posterior predictive gap for an architecture \emph{outside} the panel is
\BayesNewFam{} points $[\BayesNewFamLo{},\BayesNewFamHi{}]$,
$P(\text{gap}>0)=\BayesNewFamP{}$ --- enough to place the effect, not enough to
exclude a fourth architecture that does not show it, and under the widest prior
on the group-level scales that interval does touch zero
($\BayesWidePriorLo{}$, $P=\BayesWidePriorP{}$). Across \SpecN{} specifications
spanning every forking choice we made --- exclusion rules, $k$ threshold, cycled
against never-cycled controls, seed subset, aggregation level and outcome
definition --- the gap runs \SpecLo{}--\SpecHi{} points and none reverses its
sign (S11).

Above $k\!=\!8$ the control's fillers cycle a pool of eight, making the contrast
period-$1$ against period-$8$ rather than periodic against aperiodic.
Re-generating $k=12\ldots32$ from a never-cycled $146$-word pool leaves the
dissociation at \ApMidGap{} points (\ApMidRep{}\% against \ApMidCtl{}\%,
$n=\ApMidN{}$) where cycled controls give \ApCycGap{}: residual periodicity in
the control arm is worth \ApCost{} points, not the bulk. We quote both.

\subsection{Confirmatory: not the decoding rule, the judge, or our exclusions}

The families ship repetition penalties differing by an order of magnitude, and a
penalty suppresses repeated tokens directly. Swept on \PenNArch{} architectures
(S15) the deficit stays put --- XTTS-v2 at \PenRepLo{}--\PenRepHi{}\% exact over
a \PenFold{}-fold range, Qwen3-TTS-0.6B at \PenQRepLo{}--\PenQRepHi{}\% over
\PenQFold{}-fold --- and the \PenNoneN{} Llasa checkpoints pass \emph{no}
penalty and show it at full size, \PenNoneRep{}\% against \PenNoneCtl{}\%. Nor
is it a sampling artifact: greedy decoding gives \GreedyGap{} points against
\GreedySampGap{} sampled, at a $0$\% cap-hit rate in both arms (S22). Nor is it
our exclusions: with every rule off the gap is \ExSensAll{} points against
\ExSensPanel{} as reported (S18), and the budget rule --- the only one falling
unevenly --- removes \ExclCapRep{}\% of repeated generations against
\ExclCapCtl{}\% of controls, which works against the contrast, not for it.

Nor is it the judge, and a non-autoregressive baseline is what clears it.
VITS~\cite{kim2021vits} shows \emph{no} dissociation through the \emph{same}
recogniser on the \emph{same} strings (\VitsRep{}\% of repeated items exact
against \VitsCtl{}\% of controls, $n=90$, a gap of \VitsGap{} against the
panel's $+\ARPoolGap{}$), and not for want of competence: at
$k\!=\!6\text{--}8$, where the panel's gap reaches \ARMidGap{} points, it renders
\NonARMidRep{}\% against \NonARMidCtl{}\%, the other way round; nor for its
defaults, the sign holding at \VitsCfgWord{} duration-predictor settings (S13).
CTC blank-collapse --- the judge-side failure with the same periodicity
signature as the effect --- would have depressed VITS's repeated items too.

But F5-TTS~\cite{chen2024f5tts}, contemporary and flow-matching rather than
recurrent, \emph{does} show it: \FivettsRep{}\% against \FivettsCtl{}\%,
$+\FivettsGap{}$, growing with $k$ as the panel's does. Absence of an
autoregressive decoder confers no immunity, and we withdraw the architectural
claim an earlier draft made. What plausibly separates the two is where the count
must live: VITS gives each input token its own duration, while F5-TTS estimates
one total duration and so must represent how much speech to make. Supplying
F5-TTS the duration a correct rendering takes splits the deficit: below
$k\!=\!\DurSplit{}$ it lifts exact renderings from \DurLoFree{}\% to
\DurLoFixed{}\% ($n=\DurLoN{}$), at or above it the gain is \DurHiGain{}
($n=\DurHiN{}$). Handed the right length the model still cannot place
thirty-two repetitions inside it, so the severe end is not a duration failure
(S13). S20 sets out three rivals we cannot exclude.

\subsection{Exploratory: past the ladder, the count levels off}

Both analyses here were decided on after seeing the results above; S16 dates
every analysis decision against the commit log, and we claim little from either.

Within $k\le32$ the deficit is \emph{proportional}, not saturating: the panel
median above $k\!=\!6$ is fitted far better by $\hat c=\ShapePropSlope{}k$ than
by any constant (RSS \ShapePropSSE{} against \ShapeSatSSE{}), so no counting
horizon lies inside this ladder. On the \HzNModels{} checkpoints admitting
utterances long enough to extend it to $k\in\{48,64,96,128\}$ tracking does
stop --- but so does the controls', these decoders having a general
utterance-length ceiling, so the reportable quantity is the ratio of fitted
saturation scales: \HzRatio{}-fold, just past where the main ladder stopped,
which is why $k\le32$ looked proportional. The magnitude is form-dependent
(\HzFormLo{}--\HzFormHi{}, S17), the panel is not unanimous (\HzRevNames{}
inverts it), and a saturation scale read off counts is \emph{not} the $N^\ast$
of Section~\ref{sec:theory}: this is consistent with any saturating process.

Internally, repetition slows state acquisition without halting it: the capacity
gain --- states visited, by the trajectory's effective rank --- is a median
factor \CapRatio{} of the control's (Fig.~\ref{fig:main}(c); S8), positive in
all \CkCapN{} checkpoints. Positive is what a decoder below a horizon looks like
and equally what a decoder with none looks like.
